about: Where each end-to-end suite's cases come from. Written so the next person can tell a case derived from a published standard apart from one derived from this repo's own audit, and can find the clause to check when a case looks wrong or a spec moves.
howToUse: Adding an e2e case from a standard: cite the source id here rather than only in a code comment.
A case with no external source is fine. Say so with "internal-audit" or "regression" and name the finding or bug it pins.
This file is not generated. Update it in the same change that adds or removes a suite.

infrastructure.note: Postgres, MySQL and Valkey containers start on ephemeral ports, are seeded, and are left up for the next run to reuse. Suites skip themselves when DUCKAUTH_E2E_* is unset and docker is absent; DUCKAUTH_E2E_REQUIRE=1 makes that a failure.

rfc9700.title: RFC 9700 / BCP 240: Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
usedFor: Authorization code injection: bind every code to the client instance it was issued to.
redirect_uri compared by exact string match, never prefix or wildcard, and the code bound to the one actually used.
PKCE required for public clients and verified at the token endpoint; a missing verifier is a downgrade, not a default.
Refresh token rotation with reuse detection: a replayed token revokes the whole family.

rfc7636.title: RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients
usedFor: S256 challenge derivation, base64url(sha256(verifier)), used to build the PKCE fixtures.

owasp-session-management.title: OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet
usedFor: Regenerate the session identifier on every privilege change, which is what defeats session fixation.
Enforce idle timeout and absolute timeout as two separate deadlines, because each covers a different failure.

internal-audit.title: C1 sessions audit and the C1/C2/C4 hardening plans
usedFor: Store-contract divergences, fail-closed expiry handling, and the revocation paths the plans specify.

store-contract.title: Shared store compliance matrices
usedFor: One executable contract every adapter answers, so a dialect cannot quietly diverge.
Pointing it at a real database is what surfaced the Postgres and MySQL defects listed under regression below.

regression.title: Bugs found during this work, pinned so they cannot return
usedFor: identities.link and findByProviderSub were a SQL syntax error on Postgres (a stray bracket before ::jsonb).
credentials/identities findById leaked a raw driver error on a non-uuid id instead of returning null.
MySQL did not revive Date fields nested in json, so factors[].completedAt came back as a string.
oidc_consents carried a non-unique index, so upsert threw on Postgres and appended a duplicate row on MySQL.
MySQL code and refresh-token consume used a non-locking read, so every concurrent caller won.
verifyTotp accepted the same code indefinitely inside its ninety-second window; the spent step is now recorded on the credential.

nist-800-63b.title: NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication and Lifecycle Management
usedFor: Verifiers SHALL accept a given time-based OTP only once during its validity period. Accepting it anywhere in the drift window without spending it leaves a captured code replayable for the width of that window.

rfc6238.title: RFC 6238: TOTP, Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
usedFor: Time-step derivation and the drift window the replay check has to cover.

hostile-input.title: Adversarial input probing
usedFor: Injection payloads, prototype-pollution keys, NUL bytes, four-byte emoji, combining marks, RTL overrides, oversize values, type confusion and concurrent stampedes, against a real database rather than a Map that accepts anything.
Values that are the right type and the wrong thing: an AAL of nine, an undefined session kind, a closed impersonation window, a negative rate-limit weight, a javascript: redirect target.

owasp-asvs.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, V7 Session Management
usedFor: Session tokens carry at least 64 bits of entropy.
A new token is generated on authentication.
Tokens never appear in URL parameters.
A user can enumerate their own active sessions and end them.

owasp-forgot-password.title: OWASP Forgot Password and Authentication Cheat Sheets
usedFor: Reset tokens generated by a cryptographic RNG and long enough to resist brute force.
Reset links time limited, and rate limited per account.
Responses that do not vary by whether the account exists, in content or in timing.

rfc6749.title: RFC 6749: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
usedFor: The client_credentials grant (section 4.4) and the scope grammar (section 3.3) the m2m exchange enforces.

rfc6750.title: RFC 6750: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: Bearer Token Usage
usedFor: A client must not send a token by more than one method in one request (section 2), which is why a composite transport refuses two credentials.
The Authorization: Bearer syntax the bearer transport parses.

rfc9449.title: RFC 9449: OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)
usedFor: A proof's jti is accepted once, which is what the nonce stores enforce.
A proof-of-possession transport must not be bypassed by an unbound one composed beside it.

owasp-ssrf.title: OWASP Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet
usedFor: Refuse an outbound webhook target that reaches loopback, private or link-local space, in every spelling a URL parser accepts.

rfc4193.title: RFC 4193: Unique Local IPv6 Unicast Addresses
usedFor: fc00::/7, the IPv6 private range the webhook deny-list has to cover.

rfc4291.title: RFC 4291: IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture
usedFor: Loopback, link-local fe80::/10 and IPv4-mapped addresses, the IPv6 spellings of an inward target.

saml2-core.title: Assertions and Protocols for the OASIS Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) V2.0
usedFor: NameID and its format, the assertion ID and AuthnContextClassRef, the fields the provider reads off a response.

saml2-profiles.title: Profiles for the OASIS Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) V2.0
usedFor: The Web Browser SSO profile: RelayState returned from the request, Destination checked, and an assertion ID never accepted twice.

owasp-saml.title: OWASP SAML Security Cheat Sheet
usedFor: Replay protection, unsolicited responses, and binding a response to the request that began it.

webauthn-l3.title: Web Authentication: An API for accessing Public Key Credentials, Level 3
usedFor: Registering a New Credential (7.1): a relying party refuses a credential id already registered, because sign-in looks a credential up by that id and the id is the authenticator's to choose.
Registering a New Credential (7.1): the credential public key's algorithm is one of those registration offered in pubKeyCredParams; a verifier left to its own list takes others, SHA-1 RSA among them.
Registering a New Credential (7.1): a credential id past 1023 bytes fails registration, and sign-in takes any id up to that, so a key that registers can sign in.

Signature Counter Considerations and Verifying an Authentication Assertion (7.2): a count that does not advance, from an authenticator that counts, is a cloned authenticator; the check applies to an assertion whose signature verified.

suites.proves: A whole engine wired as an app wires it: sign-in to sign-out, the CSRF token round-tripping through the database, and the auth guard reading through the shipped queries.

Password reset, email verification and account deletion tokens work once, expire, belong to one account only, and cannot be spent across kinds. A reset revokes the account's other sessions and spares everyone else's. Sign-in refuses an unknown address with the same error as a wrong password, so it is not an enumeration oracle, and finds an account whatever the case of its address.

Injection payloads and prototype keys stay data; four-byte, combining and right-to-left unicode round-trip; a NUL byte and an empty, missing or non-string email are refused; NFC and NFD spellings of one address are one account; caps on ip, user agent, fingerprint, sid and factor count hold; wrong types and blanks are refused; the limiter never over-admits under a stampede and a hostile key stays in its own bucket; revoking a session twice is harmless, one that never existed reads as null through orNull, and touching a revoked one does not revive it; and malformed cookies resolve to null.

Values that parse cleanly but mean nothing. OIDC redirect targets refuse javascript:, data:, file: and blob: schemes, a dotless private-use scheme, userinfo, a protocol-relative target, a fragment and plain http off loopback, and admit the reverse-DNS scheme RFC 8252 asks native clients for and http to loopback. An out-of-range, zero or NaN aal, an unknown session kind and a closed impersonation window are refused as typed errors. A negative, NaN or infinite limiter weight counts as one, a fraction is floored, and any weight is spent in one round trip; a negative, NaN or absurd idempotency ttl is clamped; an empty tenant id is refused and tenant ids compare exactly.

The provider-link flow end to end, which is the caller of the two queries that were a SQL syntax error on Postgres before this audit: link, find by provider sub, idempotent relink, refusal to attach one provider account to a second identity, and the guard that refuses to unlink the last way into an account. Also the whole API key lifecycle, which had no coverage: issue, verify, revoke reaching the row, rotate killing the old secret, and the cascade on identity erase.

Every credential meant to work once does: TOTP codes are spent on use and refused on replay or rewind, backup codes are revoked on redemption, and credential rotation and revocation reach the row. No provider or flow had an e2e suite before this one.
Revocation fan-out between separate OS processes, which no in-process test can observe.
Identifier rotation on every privilege change, idle and absolute deadlines enforced separately, impersonation windows, tenant scoping, and revocation reaching the row.

Guessability, which cannot be read off a diff: session ids, CSRF tokens, API keys and reset tokens are sampled in bulk and checked for uniqueness, alphabet spread near six bits per character, absence of a shared prefix between consecutive issues, and hashed-at-rest storage. Also that no secret travels in a URL, that reset requests are rate limited per address, and that known and unknown accounts answer alike in content and in time. Issuing a new reset token retires every earlier one, and a user can list and end their own sessions without the listing carrying a secret.
The same matrix on MySQL, plus the re-SELECT that stands in for RETURNING, JSON_CONTAINS lookups, and datetime(3) precision.

The full store matrix plus dialect behaviour that exists only on Postgres: optimistic locking under real concurrency, the partial unique indexes on lower(profile->>'email') and lower(profile->>'username'), jsonb round trips, timestamptz precision, foreign keys and check constraints.

The ioredis-to-RedisLike translation this adapter exists for, where dropping EX would leave an immortal key and dropping NX would make a conditional write unconditional, checked on a real server with the rest of the surface. Also drives the whole session store contract through the adapter.
Session resolution against real queries, including that a soft-deleted identity is invisible because of the adapter's WHERE clause rather than any in-memory filtering.
Real pub/sub fan-out between separate connections, loopback dedup on the emitting instance, channel isolation and unsubscribe.
SET NX admits exactly one of many concurrent claims. FakeRedis cannot demonstrate this: its set is a Map write in one JS thread, so the race is unobservable there.
The shipped Postgres dialect: timestamptz, jsonb, uuid identity ids, and the ON DELETE CASCADE to auth_identities.

What the stored-session parser does with rows it did not write. Audit items S1, S1b and S6 are closed here by plan 02 (C1-sessions/02-sessions-redis-hardening.md); the blobs are unchanged and only the expectations moved. Seven cases pin the fail-closed reads: a null, a string, a number or an empty object inside factors now refuses the row with AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED instead of throwing out of getByHash and listByIdentity or silently leaving an aal:2 session with no factors; the sixteen-factor cap is enforced on read; and a partial actingAs envelope is refused rather than dropped, which used to cost both the audit trail and the impersonation expiry. Two companion cases prove the refusals do not cost a row sitting on the cap or a complete actingAs envelope.
The session store contract and its races on a real server rather than FakeRedis, whose own header disclaims review.
A DPoP jti replay is refused when presented to a different store instance, which is the property the store's own docstring says the memory store cannot provide.
Two instances share one counter, a twenty-way race admits exactly the configured number, and the window expires on the server rather than by a timestamp checked on read.
The provider enforces code-to-client and code-to-redirect_uri binding, PKCE verification, single-use codes under concurrency, and refresh rotation with family revoke on reuse.
The same contract on MySQL, where the concurrent-consume cases found that a non-locking read let every racer redeem the same code.
The OP store contract on Postgres. Previously only sqlite had a test and it is bun-gated, so under Node these stores were never executed.

A magic link works once and no more, eight simultaneous redemptions admit exactly one because the claim is a compare-and-set on the row version, the row is revoked in the database rather than forgotten in memory, an expired link reports distinctly, and a link minted for one identity never touches another. Also that the provider refuses a callback path that could move the authority at construction, so a typo cannot turn every future link into cross-origin token exfiltration.
Concurrent writes queued on a one-connection mysql2 pool each stamp the actor of the scope that made them, and a write outside every scope stamps no one, on create and on link alike.

The actor columns name who wrote each row across real HTTP: nobody on an anonymous request, even under a server started inside another actor's scope; the identity on a signed-in one; the operator while impersonating; and the configured default only where no session is. Concurrent requests on a one-connection pool each stamp their own actor.

The detectors decide real requests through requestSecurity: a first device steps up once and writes one suspicious event with neither the address nor the user agent in it, a deny reaction refuses before the handler runs, an impossible hop is refused until the identity is back where it was, and an onAnomaly that forgets the device refuses it again on the retry.

The siteverify call against a real HTTP peer: the form it posts, a 307 that is refused rather than re-posted with the secret, a stall before the status line or halfway through the body that times out rather than reading as malformed, a 503 that fails whatever its body says, and an HTML answer that fails as malformed.

The actor wrappers inside the frameworks they are written for rather than fakes of them: honoActorContext on a Hono app, nestActorContext applied through a Nest 12 MiddlewareConsumer behind NestExceptionFilter, expressActorContext on Express 5, koaActorContext on Koa 3, fastifyWithActor on Fastify 5, elysiaWithActor on Elysia 1.4 and withGrpc on a grpc-js server, with no error handler of the host's own except Hono's (Nest 12's default filter answers any AuthError 500). Each serves a signed-in request as its identity and an anonymous one as nobody, answers a session whose identity is gone at 401 or UNAUTHENTICATED, and raises a store outage to the framework's own error layer, the handler never running for either. Pins findings 213, 214, 216 and 221: Nest dropping the middleware, Hono answering a refusal 500, and withGrpc and the Fastify adapter not compiling against their frameworks.

The Nest handlers mounted as the example app mounts them, on a Nest 12 controller behind NestExceptionFilter on platform-express, rather than on a hand-built reply. A sign-in answers with its session and CSRF cookies and Cache-Control: no-store, and a refused one answers 401 once, with the filter leaving that answer alone and nothing logged. Pins finding 251: the filter wrote a second answer, and Nest logged ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT in place of the auth error.

The hijack policy resolves the way an operator configured it: the stronger of two reactions wins across the whole revoke/mfa/rotate/ignore matrix, a signal is still emitted when the reaction is ignore so audit keeps the record, absence on both sides is agreement, and exactly one side present drops a revoke or mfa to rotate unless onMissingSignal is strict. Diagnostic values on both sides are clipped before they reach an event. applyReaction ends the session before refusing on revoke, refuses one a concurrent request already ended, raises a store outage, and ends nothing on mfa, rotate or ignore.

The anomaly ladder holds at its boundaries and a misbehaving detector cannot take authentication down with it. The aggregate saturates, so a negative score cannot cancel a real signal and weak signals cannot sum into a deny; an id registers once; a detector that throws, hangs or emits a malformed signal is logged and skipped; every detector reads a frozen snapshot; a bus that throws leaves the deny standing; and decide agrees with evaluate over the same signals.

A device is new once per identity and stays new until a verdict lets it through, so a denied device is denied again on the retry and parallel first requests all score. The fingerprint is the user agent and the /24 or /48 alone: a stripped, padded or unparseable value cannot switch the detector off or mint a device per request, and neither the address nor the user agent reaches the evidence.

A hop faster than the configured speed scores, a sub-interval continent hop and a last-seen stamped in the future included, while a short hop inside the minimum interval, a missing or off-planet position, a non-numeric request time and a step across the antimeridian do not. Neither position reaches the evidence.

The webhook SSRF deny-list refuses loopback and private targets in every spelling: decimal, octal and hex, IPv4-mapped, NAT64 and 6to4, a fully qualified or subdomain reserved name, all of fc00::/7 and fe80::/10, and a name that resolves inward once a resolver is wired; userinfo, a non-https scheme outside the dev flag and a redirect are refused. Delivery releases the emitting flow before the retry ladder runs, stops after one attempt on a permanent 4xx or an oversize or unserialisable payload, retries a 5xx and the two 4xx codes that mean later on a jittered backoff, and blanks secret-bearing keys before signing. Signatures cover a per-delivery id and the timestamp, verify within a tolerance in either direction, and refuse an empty secret.

The client_credentials grant binds a token to the key that asked for it and to that key's tenant: a key with no tenant cannot mint for one the caller names, and a tenant-scoped key refuses another. Requested scopes are intersected with the key's and refused when nothing is left, strict mode refuses a partly-held request, the refusal names only what was asked, and the scope string is held to the RFC 6749 grammar and to length and count caps. A mismatched or empty pair, a client id differing in case, a revoked key and an over-long secret are refused. Every exchange writes an apikey session at aal 1 that expires with its token, and a transport may shorten the advertised lifetime but not extend it.

strict() reads the preset a config was branded with and demands evidence for every check the preset declares, reporting every gap in one error; a claimed limiter or lockout listener cannot stand over what the engine can see, and hipaa and fips boot once an mfa provider is registered. The resolver takes the stricter side of every field in any order, hands back fresh objects rather than the module defaults, refuses an unknown or prototype-key name, and ratchets the session windows down without lengthening one the operator set shorter. The brand survives a spread and layers without repeating.

Every verifier fails closed on what it cannot trust: a non-2xx however well its body parses, a malformed or mistyped body, a hung provider, a hostname or action that does not match, and a challenge_ts too old or too far ahead. The secret and token go in the POST body and follow no redirect, a hostile remote address is encoded, an oversized or non-string token is never relayed, and the reCAPTCHA threshold refuses a value outside 0 to 1.

Every Engine.Cfg knob createAuth accepts reaches the constructed engine: stores, transport, limiter, bus wrapped in the audit stamper, idempotency store, session windows, hijack policy, providers and org store. A plugins array, an oauth-wide state signing secret and an unknown key are refused rather than dropped, a missing store is named, and the base URL must be an absolute http(s) origin. Construction runs the production check, following NODE_ENV when no env is given and refusing an env it does not know, the string "false" included.

Registration refuses a taken id, an empty one, one that would not survive a log line or a URL, and a prototype-shaped one, registers a list whole or not at all, and has no removal. Ids match case-insensitively. list() leaves out a capability that cannot complete a sign-in, and one holding half a sign-in or nothing reachable is refused. Dispatch reaches the registered instance with this still bound, and resolve() refuses an ambiguous match rather than letting registration order pick.

The SAML provider binds a response to the request that began it: the relay state begin issued is checked on the way back, a response without one is refused unless unsolicited responses are opted into, an assertion id is consumed once so a captured body cannot be replayed, and a callbackUrl the client does not validate Destination against is refused. The assurance level comes from what the IdP asserted, and the nameID must be present, not blank, of the requested format, and match any asserted email. Limiter budget is spent on begin and complete before the verifier runs, the size cap is measured in UTF-8 bytes before the parser, and every refusal carries the same detail with the client's text kept off the wire.

CompositeTransport refuses an empty list and a request presenting two different credentials, the same token by two methods being one, with first-wins an explicit opt-in for a migration. Extract falls through past a transport that finds nothing, answers an empty string or throws on a header it cannot parse, raising that failure only when nothing else matched. Verify runs in order, caps the token before asking anyone, lets a strict transport veto rather than be fallen through past, and surfaces a fault or a falsy throw rather than reading it as nobody vouching. Issue and revoke emit every transport's intents in order, nothing when one throws, and refuse two body-emitting transports.

Every config key takes the value a caller naturally has, in one call, the way limiter already did. Idempotency accepts a one-call facet, a bare store, or an explicitly wrapped one, and wrapping twice is a no-op. Anomaly thresholds and reactions reach the facet through the engine instead of being fixed at the defaults. Guards that a later change reintroducing a wrapper step, or dropping a declared key, fails here.

The Drizzle Postgres adapter against a real server, beyond the shared matrix: identities, credentials and sessions read and write as the schema leaves them, the actor columns record who wrote and who hid a row, versioned writes refuse a lost race, erase takes credentials, sessions and links with it, and garbage in a factors or actingAs column is read as empty or refused. Every constraint the schema declares answers its typed error, with a sweep that fails on one left untested, and an unreadable value, a timed-out statement, a missing schema and an unreachable server each answer theirs. The fixture is multi-connection, so a read that ignored its transaction handle cannot hide.

withTransaction on real Postgres: a rollback leaves no identity, session or credential row and publishes no event, a commit publishes only on flush, a read inside the transaction sees its own write, a nested flow inherits the caller's transaction, one bad row rolls a batch back while a soft failure does not, and the unbound engine still commits and emits on its own.
valkeyEvents over real pub/sub: an emit on one instance reaches a listener on another, and the emitting instance does not see its own emit twice.

origin and fleet delivery over real pub/sub: an origin handler runs once, on the emitter, inside its async context, a fleet handler runs on every server and outside it on a peer, origin handlers hold no channel, and an emit publishes from a server with no fleet handler.
valkeyIdempotency on a real server: a second call inside the window replays the first response, and exactly one of many concurrent claims executes.
valkeySessionImpl round-trips and deletes a session on a real server.
valkeyDPoPNonceStore on a real server accepts a jti once and refuses the replay, including one presented on a different connection.
valkeyLimiter on a real server counts down to zero and then refuses, and two instances share one counter.
RedisPasskeyChallengeStore on a real server hands a challenge back once across instances, admits one of twenty simultaneous takes, and leaves expiry to the server.

Passkeys and WebAuthn MFA on real Postgres, signed by a software authenticator and checked by the real verifier: a registered passkey signs its owner in and its count lands on the row; a signed rollback is refused and reported and a forged assertion refused unreported; a credential id another account already holds is refused at registration on both paths, so its owner keeps signing in.
